context: civil-heavy watertight structures · two-stage (clean-water then biological) commissioning

brief.intro: New to this project type? A water or wastewater treatment plant is civil-heavy in a way most other industrial types are not: the watertight concrete tanks, basins and clarifiers, and the buried inlet/outlet pipework, are themselves the enabling long-lead scope — not just a foundation for the mechanical fit-out. Pumps, blowers, mixers and dosing skids are the mechanical/process core, and instrumentation ties it together through SCADA/PLC. The defining planning rule is that commissioning runs in two stages: clean-water functional testing first, then dirty-water/biological seeding against a regulatory discharge consent — a back-loaded, compliance-gated finish where the biological process itself needs real, non-compressible time to establish.

glossary.plain: proving a concrete tank or basin doesn't leak before it's put into service.
the wet well holds incoming flow; the dry well houses the pumps that lift it, kept dry and separate.
running pumps, valves and dosing systems on plain water before real sewage or process water is introduced.
introducing the bacteria culture that actually does the treatment work, and giving it time to establish.
the regulator's permit setting the water-quality limits the plant must meet before treated water can be released.
the control system and its logic controllers that run pumps, valves, dosing and alarms automatically.
advanced treatment stages — filtration membranes, ultraviolet disinfection, or reverse osmosis — each needing its own performance verification.

must_get_right: Watertight concrete basins and buried pipework are the true long-lead, enabling scope — protect their concrete cure and watertightness-test time, not just the mechanical fit-out that follows.
Commissioning is two-stage — clean-water first, then dirty-water/biological seeding — never collapse them into one step, and hold real time for biological seeding to establish before consent testing.
The discharge-consent compliance test, not mechanical completion, is the true finish line — build in time for sampling and regulator sign-off.
Sequence civil (watertightness proven) before mechanical fit-out (pumps/blowers/dosing) inside every tank or basin.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil concrete pours are sequenced around curing time rather than a simple days-per-week rate; mechanical and electrical fit-out run a single-shift 6-day week; the commissioning phase extends over several weeks to allow biological seeding to establish before consent sampling begins.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs water-retaining structure concrete → cure → watertightness test → mechanical/process fit-out → electrical & SCADA → clean-water commissioning → biological seeding → consent compliance sampling → handover. The biological seeding/establishment period is a fixed, non-compressible duration and is the true schedule driver at the back end.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen; geotechnical and groundwater conditions are as reported (dewatering allowed for); the discharge-consent limits are agreed with the regulator ahead of commissioning; and a single mobilisation. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule carries genuine procurement long-leads alongside the civil scope. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Dewatering is often required during excavation and concrete works; wet-well/dry-well and confined-space entry needs permitted access; large blowers and tanks require crane access; and tie-ins to an existing sewer network, watercourse or operating plant are coordinated with the operator/regulator in advance.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: watertightness-test failures and rework, biological-seeding delays (temperature- and loading-dependent), consent-sampling re-test loops, and groundwater/dewatering risk during civil works. Schedule contingency is held immediately before biological seeding and before consent compliance testing rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
